subject: Concerns about parking restrictions – impact on elderly worshippers
body: Dear Council Members, I am writing to express my concerns about the proposed parking restrictions outside the Mandir. I rely on accessible parking close to the Mandir. The Mandir is regularly visited by elderly devotees, people with limited mobility, and families with young children. Easy, nearby parking is essential for them. Paid parking and permit restrictions create a physical and financial barrier that may prevent some community members from attending altogether. For those of us with mobility limitations, the ability to park nearby is not a convenience but a fundamental requirement for continued participation in religious practice. People with disabilities or limited mobility cannot walk long distances and have no alternative to parking nearby. Furthermore, if parking directly outside the Mandir becomes paid and permit-restricted, visitors will look for free alternatives further away. This is likely to push parking deeper into nearby residential roads beyond the permit zone, increasing congestion and causing frustration for local residents—the opposite of what the policy may intend. Rather than solving parking issues, this proposal will merely displace them to other streets, creating additional problems for residential areas. It is crucial to recognise that the Mandir is not just a place of worship but a key community centre offering cultural, educational, and charitable activities. Policies affecting it should reflect this wider social value and be designed to support, not hinder, community participation. Unlike typical parking issues, places of worship serve regional communities, not just immediate neighbourhoods. A permit-based system that prioritises residential parking does not account for the unique nature and social value of community facilities like the Mandir. I urge you to reconsider this proposal and take into account the impact on vulnerable community members and the broader social value of the Mandir. Yours sincerely

subject: Objection to parking charges near Mandir
body: Dear Members of the Council, I wish to raise my objections to the proposed pay-per-hour parking and permit scheme near the Mandir. Mandir visits are not time-bound. Darshan, prayer, meditation, satsang, and seva often take varying amounts of time. Pay-per-hour parking places pressure on worshippers to rush or leave early, which is not compatible with religious observance. Even if permits are available, they are typically tied to residential addresses and would not be accessible to the majority of Mandir visitors who travel from across a wide geographical area. This fundamentally undermines the nature of spiritual practice, which cannot be constrained by parking meters. Many devotees attend the Mandir multiple times a week. Even modest hourly charges quickly add up, creating a recurring cost for people who are simply practising their faith or volunteering their time. Permit schemes typically only benefit local residents, leaving regular worshippers from other areas with no affordable option. The cumulative effect of regular parking charges—even if individually small—can become prohibitive over time. For someone attending multiple times per week, annual parking costs could run into hundreds of pounds simply to practise their faith. Moreover, places of worship play an important social and cultural role and should be accessible to all, regardless of economic circumstances or residential location. Parking charges and permit restrictions risk excluding several vulnerable groups, including lower-income families who may struggle with recurring parking costs, elderly residents and pensioners on fixed incomes for whom even modest charges represent a significant recurring expense, and worshippers from outside the permit area who form the majority of the congregation and would have no access to resident permits. This creates a two-tier system where only those who can afford to pay or who happen to live locally have full access to their place of worship, fundamentally undermining the principles of inclusivity and equal access that underpin community cohesion and religious freedom. I respectfully request that you reconsider this proposal. Yours faithfully

subject: Parking restrictions impact on Mandir volunteers
body: To the Council, I am writing regarding the proposed parking charges and permit restrictions outside the Mandir. The Mandir depends on volunteers for daily operations, cleaning, food preparation, teaching, and event support. Parking charges and permit restrictions may discourage volunteers from attending as frequently, directly affecting the Mandir's ability to serve the community. Many volunteers travel from outside the immediate area and would not qualify for permits. Without the dedication of volunteers who freely give their time, the Mandir simply cannot function effectively. Asking volunteers to pay for parking whilst they serve the community adds an unreasonable financial burden to those already contributing their time and effort. This will inevitably lead to lower attendance and reduced volunteer presence, which can also affect donations and participation. These are essential for maintaining community services, charitable work, and outreach programmes. The financial sustainability of the Mandir depends on active community engagement, which these parking restrictions would severely undermine. The Mandir provides vital services that benefit the wider community, and anything that threatens volunteer participation threatens these services. I would also emphasise that the Mandir is not just a place of worship but a key community centre offering cultural, educational, and charitable activities. Policies affecting it should reflect this wider social value and be designed to support, not hinder, community participation. Unlike typical parking issues, places of worship serve regional communities, not just immediate neighbourhoods. A permit-based system that prioritises residential parking does not account for the unique nature and social value of community facilities like the Mandir. Community hubs like the Mandir deserve policy considerations that recognise their broader contribution to social cohesion and community wellbeing. I urge the Council to reconsider this proposal and recognise the vital community role the Mandir plays. Kind regards

subject: Parking charges – concerns for families with children
body: Dear Council, I am writing to object to the introduction of pay-per-hour parking and permit restrictions near the Mandir. The Mandir is regularly visited by families with young children, and easy, nearby parking is essential for them. Paid parking and permit restrictions create both a physical and financial barrier that may prevent some families from attending altogether. Managing children whilst having to park far away is simply not practical and, in many cases, creates safety concerns. Families with young children require accessible parking as a practical necessity, not merely a preference. Additionally, large gatherings such as festivals, sabhas, weddings, funerals, and cultural events rely heavily on accessible parking. Introducing paid bays and permit restrictions is likely to reduce attendance, particularly for families and those travelling from further away who would not be eligible for resident permits. These events are central to our community life and cultural identity. They provide opportunities for families to connect with their culture and for children to learn about their heritage. Anything that reduces attendance at these events undermines community cohesion and cultural continuity. The financial aspect cannot be ignored either. Many devotees attend the Mandir multiple times a week, and even modest hourly charges quickly add up, creating a recurring cost for people who are simply practising their faith or volunteering their time. Permit schemes typically only benefit local residents, leaving regular worshippers from other areas with no affordable option. For families already managing the costs of raising children, these additional recurring charges represent a significant burden. Lower-income families may struggle with recurring parking costs, particularly if visiting multiple times per week. These proposals would place an unfair burden on families who wish to participate in their faith and community. I ask that you reconsider and seek alternative solutions that do not exclude families from accessing the Mandir. Yours sincerely

subject: Concerns about parking displacement near Mandir
body: To Whom It May Concern, I am writing as a local resident to express concern about the proposed parking restrictions near the Mandir. Whilst I understand the intention may be to manage parking, I fear the policy will have the opposite effect. If parking directly outside the Mandir becomes paid and permit-restricted, visitors will look for free alternatives further away. This is likely to push parking deeper into nearby residential roads beyond the permit zone, increasing congestion and causing frustration for local residents—the opposite of what the policy may intend. Rather than solving the parking issue, this proposal will simply displace it to other streets, spreading the problem across a wider residential area. The burden on residents in streets further from the Mandir may actually increase as visitors seek free parking alternatives. Additionally, drivers may circle the area looking for cheaper or free parking outside the permit zone, increasing traffic, noise, and emissions in the immediate neighbourhood and surrounding areas. This will negatively impact the quality of life for residents and contribute to environmental degradation. The increased traffic and pollution would affect not just those living immediately adjacent to the Mandir, but the wider residential area as vehicles circulate searching for parking. This additional traffic serves no purpose other than to avoid parking charges, yet creates tangible harm through increased noise, air pollution, and congestion. These unintended consequences suggest that the proposed policy has not been fully thought through. A policy that displaces rather than solves parking issues and that increases traffic and emissions cannot be considered successful. I urge the Council to reconsider and consult more broadly with both the Mandir community and local residents to find a solution that genuinely addresses parking concerns without creating new problems. Yours sincerely

Pay-per-hour parking places pressure on worshippers to rush or leave early, which is not compatible with religious observance. Even if permits are available, they are typically tied to residential addresses and would not be accessible to the majority of Mandir visitors who travel from across a wide geographical area. The combination of physical difficulty and time pressure would make attendance nearly impossible for many elderly devotees. For those who may move more slowly and need more time for prayer and rest, the pressure of parking meters is particularly burdensome and incompatible with comfortable and meaningful participation in worship. These barriers would effectively exclude elderly community members from religious practice and community participation, which is both discriminatory and harmful to community cohesion. I respectfully request that you reconsider this proposal. Yours sincerely

subject: Objection to parking charges near Mandir
body: To Whom It May Concern, I am writing regarding the proposed parking charges and permit restrictions outside the Mandir. Many devotees attend the Mandir multiple times a week. Even modest hourly charges quickly add up, creating a recurring cost for people who are simply practising their faith or volunteering their time. Permit schemes typically only benefit local residents, leaving regular worshippers from other areas with no affordable option. The cumulative financial burden would be significant for those who attend frequently. The cumulative effect of regular parking charges—even if individually small—can become prohibitive over time. For someone attending multiple times per week, annual parking costs could run into hundreds of pounds simply to practise their faith. This creates a financial barrier to religious practice that is both unreasonable and discriminatory. Additionally, the Mandir depends on volunteers for daily operations, cleaning, food preparation, teaching, and event support. Parking charges and permit restrictions may discourage volunteers from attending as frequently, directly affecting the Mandir's ability to serve the community. Many volunteers travel from outside the immediate area and would not qualify for permits. I would face a double burden from these charges—paying to practise my faith and paying to volunteer my time in service to the community. This is fundamentally unfair and will discourage the civic engagement and community service that volunteers provide. These proposals would place an unfair financial burden on those who are most active in the community and who contribute most to its vitality and sustainability. I ask that you reconsider. Yours respectfully

subject: Parking restrictions impact on Mandir volunteers
body: Dear Council Members, I write to object to the proposed pay-per-hour parking and permit restrictions near the Mandir. The Mandir depends on volunteers for daily operations, cleaning, food preparation, teaching, and event support. Parking charges and permit restrictions may discourage volunteers from attending as frequently, directly affecting the Mandir's ability to serve the community. Many volunteers travel from outside the immediate area and would not qualify for permits. Volunteers already give their time freely; asking them to also pay for parking whilst they serve the community is unreasonable and will inevitably reduce volunteer participation. The Mandir's operations depend entirely on volunteer labour, and anything that discourages volunteering threatens the Mandir's ability to function and serve the community. Furthermore, Mandir visits are not time-bound. Darshan, prayer, meditation, satsang, and seva often take varying amounts of time. Pay-per-hour parking places pressure on worshippers to rush or leave early, which is not compatible with religious observance. Even if permits are available, they are typically tied to residential addresses and would not be accessible to the majority of Mandir visitors who travel from across a wide geographical area. Volunteering sessions can last several hours, and the accumulated parking charges would be particularly burdensome. A volunteer who serves for three or four hours could face parking charges of several pounds each time, which quickly adds up when volunteering regularly. This financial burden on top of the time commitment is unreasonable. Volunteering is the foundation of community cohesion and civic engagement. Policies should support and encourage volunteering, not create financial barriers to it. I urge the Council to reconsider this proposal and recognise the contribution volunteers make to the community. Yours sincerely

subject: Parking charges – concerns for families with children
body: Dear Sir or Madam, I am writing to express my opposition to the proposed parking charges and permit restrictions near the Mandir. Large gatherings such as festivals, sabhas, weddings, funerals, and cultural events rely heavily on accessible parking. Introducing paid bays and permit restrictions is likely to reduce attendance, particularly for families and those travelling from further away who would not be eligible for resident permits. These events are important for families to maintain cultural connections and community bonds. They provide essential opportunities for children to learn about their culture and heritage, for families to connect with their community, and for social support networks to be maintained. Reduced attendance would weaken these vital community functions. Additionally, many devotees attend the Mandir multiple times a week. Even modest hourly charges quickly add up, creating a recurring cost for people who are simply practising their faith or participating in community events. Permit schemes typically only benefit local residents, leaving families from other areas with no affordable option. For families already managing the costs of raising children, these additional charges represent a significant burden. The cumulative effect of regular parking charges—even if individually small—can become prohibitive over time. Lower-income families may struggle with recurring parking costs, particularly if visiting multiple times per week. For a family attending once or twice a week for religious services and children's classes, the annual parking costs could amount to hundreds of pounds. This represents a significant expense for families already managing childcare, education, and household costs. The financial burden would be particularly acute for larger families and those on limited incomes. These proposals would make it difficult for families to participate fully in their faith community and would undermine the cultural transmission to the next generation. I ask that you reconsider. Yours faithfully

subject: Opposition to parking charges – financial burden on low-income worshippers
body: To the Council, I wish to object to the proposed parking charges and permit restrictions outside the Mandir. Many devotees attend the Mandir multiple times a week. Even modest hourly charges quickly add up, creating a recurring cost for people who are simply practising their faith or volunteering their time. Permit schemes typically only benefit local residents, leaving regular worshippers from other areas with no affordable option. For those on limited incomes, these costs can become prohibitive. The cumulative effect of regular parking charges—even if individually small—can become prohibitive over time. For someone attending multiple times per week, annual parking costs could run into hundreds of pounds simply to practise their faith. This financial barrier discriminates against those on lower incomes and effectively excludes them from religious practice. Moreover, Mandir visits are not time-bound. Darshan, prayer, meditation, satsang, and seva often take varying amounts of time. Pay-per-hour parking places pressure on worshippers to rush or leave early, which is not compatible with religious observance. Even if permits are available, they are typically tied to residential addresses and would not be accessible to the majority of Mandir visitors who travel from across a wide geographical area. The combination of financial burden and time pressure would fundamentally interfere with religious practice. Those on limited incomes would face impossible choices: either incur parking charges they cannot afford, or rush their worship to minimise costs, or simply stop attending altogether. Permit systems, whilst protecting local residents, do nothing to address the needs of a place of worship that serves a wide community. This creates a two-tier system where only those who can afford to pay or who happen to live locally have full access to their place of worship. I respectfully ask that you reconsider this proposal and ensure that places of worship remain accessible to all. Yours sincerely

subject: Parking restrictions – impact on community events and gatherings
body: Dear Council, I am writing regarding the proposed pay-per-hour parking and permit restrictions near the Mandir. The Mandir is not just a place of worship but a key community centre offering cultural, educational, and charitable activities. Policies affecting it should reflect this wider social value and be designed to support, not hinder, community participation. Unlike typical parking issues, places of worship serve regional communities, not just immediate neighbourhoods. A permit-based system that prioritises residential parking does not account for the unique nature and social value of community facilities like the Mandir. The Mandir provides services that benefit the wider community including educational programmes, cultural activities, charitable support, and social cohesion initiatives. These services serve people from across a wide geographical area, not just the immediate neighbourhood. Furthermore, the Mandir depends on volunteers for daily operations, cleaning, food preparation, teaching, and event support. Parking charges and permit restrictions may discourage volunteers from attending as frequently, directly affecting the Mandir's ability to serve the community. Many volunteers travel from outside the immediate area and would not qualify for permits. Without volunteers, the community programmes and services that the Mandir provides simply cannot continue. The entire infrastructure of community services depends on volunteer participation, which these parking restrictions would severely undermine. Community facilities like the Mandir are essential for social cohesion, cultural continuity, and community wellbeing. They provide spaces for social connection, mutual support, and cultural transmission that cannot be replicated elsewhere. Policies should recognise and support these vital community functions rather than creating barriers to participation. I urge the Council to recognise the Mandir's vital community role and reconsider this proposal. Yours respectfully

subject: Concerns about parking displacement near Mandir
body: Dear Members of the Council, I write as a local resident to express concern about the proposed parking restrictions near the Mandir. If parking directly outside the Mandir becomes paid and permit-restricted, visitors will look for free alternatives further away. This is likely to push parking deeper into nearby residential roads beyond the permit zone, increasing congestion and causing frustration for local residents—the opposite of what the policy may intend. This predictable displacement effect will spread parking pressure across a wider residential area, creating problems in streets that currently have adequate parking availability. Additionally, drivers may circle the area looking for cheaper or free parking outside the permit zone, increasing traffic, noise, and emissions in the immediate neighbourhood and surrounding areas. This will reduce the quality of life for residents and contribute to environmental degradation. The additional traffic serves no purpose beyond avoiding parking charges, yet creates real harm through increased noise, air pollution, and congestion in residential streets. It is important to recognise that the Mandir is not just a place of worship but a key community centre offering cultural, educational, and charitable activities. Policies affecting it should reflect this wider social value and be designed to support, not hinder, community participation. Unlike typical parking issues, places of worship serve regional communities, not just immediate neighbourhoods. A permit-based system that prioritises residential parking does not account for the unique nature and social value of community facilities like the Mandir. A more collaborative approach is needed that balances the needs of residents with the important role the Mandir plays in the community. Solutions should address the underlying issues rather than simply displacing problems to other areas. I ask that you reconsider this proposal. Yours sincerely

subject: Objection to parking scheme on environmental grounds
body: Dear Council, I wish to object to the proposed parking charges and permit restrictions near the Mandir on environmental and sustainability grounds. Drivers may circle the area looking for cheaper or free parking outside the permit zone, increasing traffic, noise, and emissions in the immediate neighbourhood and surrounding areas. This undermines environmental objectives and increases pollution. The additional vehicle movements represent a step backwards in terms of air quality and carbon emissions. This represents entirely avoidable traffic, generated solely by the parking policy itself, which serves no transport purpose beyond avoiding charges. From an environmental perspective, policy-induced traffic is particularly problematic as it creates pollution with no offsetting benefit. The environmental harm is entirely avoidable through better policy design. Furthermore, lower attendance and reduced volunteer presence resulting from parking restrictions can affect donations and participation, which are essential for maintaining community services, charitable work, and outreach programmes. Community facilities like the Mandir contribute to social sustainability, which is an important aspect of overall environmental and community wellbeing. Undermining the Mandir's sustainability runs counter to broader sustainability goals. Social sustainability—the maintenance of social capital, community cohesion, and support networks—is an essential component of overall sustainability alongside environmental and economic sustainability. Policies that undermine social sustainability in the name of parking management are shortsighted and fail to recognise the interconnected nature of environmental, social, and economic wellbeing. Environmental policy should take a holistic view that considers vehicle emissions, community facility sustainability, and social cohesion together. Sustainable communities require both environmental protection and strong social infrastructure. I ask that you reconsider this proposal from a holistic sustainability perspective. Yours respectfully

subject: Parking charges – financial barrier for students and young people
body: To Whom It May Concern, I am writing to object to the proposed parking charges and permit restrictions outside the Mandir. Many devotees, including students and young people, attend the Mandir multiple times a week. Even modest hourly charges quickly add up, creating a recurring cost that students can ill afford. Permit schemes typically only benefit local residents, leaving young people from other areas with no affordable option. This would effectively exclude students from participating in youth activities at the Mandir. The cumulative effect of regular parking charges—even if individually small—can become prohibitive over time. For someone attending multiple times per week, annual parking costs could run into hundreds of pounds simply to practise their faith. For those already managing tuition fees, accommodation costs, and living expenses, these additional recurring parking charges represent a burden we simply cannot afford. Additionally, large gatherings such as festivals, sabhas, and cultural events rely heavily on accessible parking. Introducing paid bays and permit restrictions is likely to reduce attendance, particularly for young people travelling from further away who would not be eligible for resident permits. Cultural events are important for young people to connect with their heritage and community, and reducing attendance would undermine this. These events provide essential opportunities for young people to learn about their culture, connect with their community, and develop their identity. They are not optional extras but fundamental to cultural transmission and community belonging. Students and young people are the future of the community, and policies should support rather than hinder their participation in cultural and religious life. Creating financial barriers to youth participation undermines the long-term sustainability of the community. I urge the Council to reconsider this proposal. Yours sincerely

subject: Parking restrictions – impact on cultural events and community cohesion
body: Dear Council Members, I write to express my objection to the proposed pay-per-hour parking and permit restrictions near the Mandir. Large gatherings such as festivals, sabhas, weddings, funerals, and cultural events rely heavily on accessible parking. Introducing paid bays and permit restrictions is likely to reduce attendance, particularly for families and those travelling from further away who would not be eligible for resident permits. They serve as vital occasions for bringing together community members, strengthening social bonds, passing cultural traditions to younger generations, and providing mutual support. The social value of these events extends far beyond the immediate participants to benefit the wider community through enhanced social cohesion. Places of worship play an important social and cultural role and should be accessible to all, regardless of economic circumstances or residential location. Parking charges and permit restrictions risk excluding several vulnerable groups. Lower-income families may struggle with recurring parking costs, particularly for events they wish to attend. Worshippers from outside the permit area who form the majority of the congregation would have no access to resident permits. The cumulative effect of regular parking charges—even if individually small—can become prohibitive over time. For families who wish to attend multiple events throughout the year, the accumulated parking charges could amount to significant sums. Permit systems, whilst protecting local residents, do nothing to address the needs of a place of worship that serves a wide community. This creates a two-tier system where only those who can afford to pay or who happen to live locally have full access to their place of worship, fundamentally undermining the principles of inclusivity and equal access that underpin community cohesion and religious freedom. I respectfully ask that you reconsider this proposal. Yours faithfully
